questions.stem: Gary, a 56-year-old builder in ED with severe epigastric pain going through to his back, tells you he drinks 4 full-strength stubbies a night and had about 12 at a party last night. He is likely to be admitted for several days. Which history question best assesses his immediate risk of alcohol withdrawal on the ward?
options: "How many standard drinks do you have on a typical day, and what do you usually drink?"
"Have you ever felt annoyed when people criticise your drinking?"
"When was your last drink, and have you had shakes, fits or hallucinations off it?"
"Has anyone in your family ever had a problem with alcohol or other drugs?"
questions.why: The time of the last drink tells you when withdrawal is likely (usually 6 to 24 hours after it), and past shakes, seizures or hallucinations are the strongest predictors of severe withdrawal. Record both, then monitor with a withdrawal scale.
notes: Daily intake helps judge dependence, but it does not tell you when withdrawal will start or whether he has had severe withdrawal before.
This is a CAGE screening item for problem drinking. It does not tell you when withdrawal will happen or how severe it might be.
Family history of alcohol problems adds to long-term risk but tells you nothing about withdrawal over the next few days.

questions.stem: Gary, 56, has acute alcohol-related pancreatitis. In ED his HR has risen from 109 to 114, he has vomited again and has passed no urine since arrival. Haematocrit is 0.52, and creatinine, BP, SpO2 and lactate are normal. What is the most appropriate IV fluid plan?
options: Hartmann's bolus, reassess, then titrate the rate to urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h
Hartmann's 20 mL/kg bolus, then a fixed 3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours regardless of urine output
5% glucose at 125 mL/h as maintenance until he can drink again
Hold IV fluids and give oral fluids until his creatinine starts to rise
questions.why: Use goal-directed balanced crystalloid in pancreatitis: give a moderate bolus, reassess, then titrate to haemodynamics and a urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/h. Aggressive fixed high-volume regimens cause fluid overload and do not improve outcomes.
notes: An aggressive fixed regimen like this caused more fluid overload with no benefit in the WATERFALL trial, so it is no longer recommended.
5% glucose is hypotonic maintenance fluid, not resuscitation fluid, and in a heavy drinker glucose should not be given before thiamine.
He is already tachycardic, haemoconcentrated and not passing urine. Waiting for the creatinine to rise means waiting for organ failure.

questions.stem: Gary, 56, has a lipase of 1850 U/L after a heavy binge on top of daily drinking. Ultrasound shows a bulky, oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid and no gallstones. What is the central initiating event in the pathogenesis of acute pancreatitis?
options: Ascending bacterial infection of the pancreatic duct from the duodenum
Ischaemia of the pancreas from atherosclerosis of the coeliac trunk
Autoimmune destruction of acinar cells by circulating autoantibodies
Premature activation of trypsinogen to trypsin within the acinar cells
questions.why: Trypsinogen activated too early inside acinar cells (alcohol makes acinar cells more prone to this) activates other enzymes and causes autodigestion. The cytokine release that follows explains SIRS and capillary leak.
notes: Pancreatitis starts as sterile inflammation. Infection, if it happens at all, is a late complication of necrosis, which is why prophylactic antibiotics are not given.
Ischaemia is a rare cause (for example after cardiac bypass) and does not explain pancreatitis after a binge in someone with a normal lactate.
Autoimmune pancreatitis is an uncommon IgG4-related condition with a subacute course. It does not cause sudden pancreatitis after drinking.

questions.stem: Gary, 56, describes constant epigastric pain going straight through to his back, eased a little by leaning forward. On ultrasound, bowel gas partly obscured the view of his pancreas. Which description of the pancreas's position best explains why the pain radiates to the back?
options: Intraperitoneal, in the greater omentum in front of the transverse colon
Retroperitoneal, on the posterior abdominal wall at L1–L2 behind the stomach
Retroperitoneal, at T10–T11 directly behind the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm
Intraperitoneal, within the lesser omentum between the stomach and liver
questions.why: The pancreas (except the tail) is retroperitoneal. It lies across L1–L2 behind the stomach and lesser sac, close to the coeliac plexus, so inflammation is felt in the back. The stomach and colon in front of it are also why bowel gas limits ultrasound views.
notes: The pancreas is not in the greater omentum. An organ hanging in front of the colon would not cause pain through to the back.
This level is too high. The pancreas lies at about L1–L2, below the oesophageal hiatus (T10), and its body crosses in front of the aorta and the origin of the SMA.
The lesser omentum carries the hepatic portal triad, not the pancreas, which lies behind the lesser sac on the posterior abdominal wall.
